### Reviewer 4

The manuscript addresses the urgent need to improve constraints on observed aerosol properties
for understanding aerosol direct and indirect effects on climate, both from the pre-industrial period
until now and for future climate projections. Rather than using a traditional physics-based forward
model to perform the retrieval of aerosol properties, the manuscript proposes to use a feedforward,
fully connected neural network (NN), a novel application in this specific domain. Specifically, the
NN uses plane-based lidar observations (supplemented with reanalysis products) to predict CCN
concentration and aerosol absorption (ABS). The manuscript argues this machine learning model
can be applied to future satellite lidar observations with appropriate adjustments to input data
(restricting wavelengths of lidar data used as model inputs and adding random noise).
This work demonstrates the major potential of machine learning and lidar observations to
revolutionize retrievals of vertically resolved aerosol properties. However, the results currently
presented seem to be a stepping stone toward revolutionary aerosol retrievals rather than a fait
accompli. The manuscript at present does not include enough information about data
measurement and processing and associated variability/uncertainty to access whether this
represents an significant additional source of uncertainty presently unaccounted for (major issue
1). The machine learning models show substantial biases in their predictions of aerosol properties
under clean conditions, which are important for estimating climate impacts (major issue 2). Finally,
the manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate that the models trained on plane lidar data are
transferable to satellite lidar data with only restrictions in inputs and additional input noise (major
issue 3). The combination of the issues makes it difficult to evaluate the manuscript’s claim that
they demonstrate machine learning can substantially improve observationally inferred aerosol
properties relative to present physics-based retrievals.
Major issue 1: Data processing and its associated uncertainties are not adequately described.
The manuscript does not appear to include information on the instruments and processing
performed to produce the predicted aerosol properties of CCN and ABS. The co-location procedure
used to combine in-situ aerosol measurements and lidar profiles is also very sparsely described.
Why were the distance and time values used chosen? How sensitive are the distributions of CCN
and ABS data to these choices? (Independent of the ML predictions, the distribution of in-situ
points in Figure 2 vs Figure S2 look non-trivially different.) How are multiple observations satisfying
co-location requirements combined? What kind variability is present among multiple
observations? The text should at least mention and ideally estimate the magnitude of
uncertainty/variability introduced by the co-location and data processing algorithms as well as
typical instrument errors and counting uncertainties.
Major issue 2: The models presented show strong biases as a function of aerosol absorption and
concentration.
Figures 2 and 4 show clear biases in overestimating both CCN and ABS at low values. These biases
are not mentioned in the manuscript text and seem to have limited effect on the metrics used to
quantify the performance of the NN models because most data points appear to be clustered at
intermediate values of CCN and ABS. (This is difficult to say quantitatively because density of
points in Figure 2 and 4 are not given and Figure 1 only includes distributions of occurrence
frequency of CCN and ABS in each campaign, not the full dataset.) This bias is particularly
concerning because better constraints on aerosol properties in clean conditions are needed to
reduce uncertainty in aerosol-cloud indirect effects important for climate (Gryspeerdt et al., 2023,
https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-23-4115-2023).
Major issue 3: The manuscript does not convincingly demonstrate the transferability of the
presented models based on aircraft observations to satellite observations.
Sensitivity test 2 (Figure S3) suggests (unsurprisingly) that the NN models have no capacity to
extrapolate. The manuscript does not address the extrapolations likely to be encountered when
applying four limited-area field campaigns to global data. While sensitivity test 3 (Figure S4)
demonstrates that the NN models can interpolate between values under conditions seen in the
field campaigns, it does not show the transferability of the NN models to different meteorological or
aerosol conditions outside what was seen in the field campaigns. Additionally, while manuscript
considers restricting lidar input data and random noise to address differences between airborne
and satellite measurements, the manuscript does not address differences in airborne and satellite
lidar instrument systematics as well as their observing profiles, resolutions, and coverages.
minor comments:
Figure 1: An additional row of histograms with data from all campaigns would be helpful. The
reanalysis products (RH, T) used in some NNs should also be included in these histograms.
Figures 2 and 4: Missing colorbars to quantify densities. I find the scatter point-based density
difficult to interpret. What range of values does each point encompass?
Figure 6: Missing description of white points (appears to be some retrieval of cloud top). Missing
description of how blacked out portions determined. I would recommend using a perceptually
uniform colormap over jet.
Text does not explain selection of T and RH as the reanalysis quantities chosen to include to
improve predictions. References should be included to justify why these properties are physically
predictive. Ideally some analysis would be included to show that T and RH are not being using by
the NN to distinguish different campaigns, leading to spurious relationships over a broader range of
measurements.
While the NN hyper parameter ranges searched are presented in the Table S2, I don’t see the hyper
parameters used for the presented results anywhere. These should be included somewhere to
inform (among other things) the number of trainable parameters vs the number of training points.
Code repository does not appear to include data processing and NN training, validation, and hyper
parameter tuning.

The code to generate figures is present in the listed repository, but the repository does not appear to
include co-location data processing and NN training, validation, and hyper parameter tuning.
